body_edits.diff:
Under NIST [sp800-63b, 4.3](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/events/#loss-theft-damage-and-compromise) you find the following paragraph:

"CSPs MAY support the temporary suspension of authenticators that are suspected of possible compromise. If suspension is supported, it SHOULD be reversed after the subscriber successfully authenticates to the CSP using a valid (i.e., not suspended) authenticator and requests reactivation of the suspended authenticator. The CSP MAY set a time limit after which a suspended authenticator can no longer be reactivated."

Currently we have:

6.4.4 | Verify that if a multi-factor authentication factor is lost, evidence of identity proofing is performed at the same level as during enrollment. | 2
-- | -- | --

What I believe is missing is the suspension and reversal of the suspension that currently isn't mentioned in ASVS.

Please also note the passage in 4.2.2.3: "f an account that can authenticate at AAL3 has been identity-proofed at IAL1 or IAL2, the requirements are the same as those for recovery at AAL2" and so on.

Under NIST [sp800-63b, 4.3](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/events/#loss-theft-damage-and-compromise) you find the following paragraph:

"CSPs MAY support the temporary suspension of authenticators that are suspected of possible compromise. If suspension is supported, it SHOULD be reversed after the subscriber successfully authenticates to the CSP using a valid (i.e., not suspended) authenticator and requests reactivation of the suspended authenticator. The CSP MAY set a time limit after which a suspended authenticator can no longer be reactivated."

Currently we have:

6.4.4 | Verify that if a multi-factor authentication factor is lost, evidence of identity proofing is performed at the same level as during enrollment. | 2
-- | -- | --

What I believe is missing is the suspension and reversal of the suspension that currently isn't mentioned in ASVS.

Please also note the passage in [4.2.2.3](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/events/#recovery-at-aal3): "If an account that can authenticate at AAL3 has been identity-proofed at IAL1 or IAL2, the requirements are the same as those for recovery at AAL2" and so on.

I believe activation of out-of-bound authenticators like devices or cards are refered to in "4.1.2.2: Binding Across Endpoints": https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/events/#binding-across-endpoints
In NIST terms, authenticator activation can be referred to as "binding".
There are use cases where devices like FIDO keys or cards are given physically to users. In those cases, they are not bound to the user's accounts before the user receives them. In those cases, activation codes may be necessary. Therefore, I propose the following:

On suspicion of compromise, an authenticator, such as a device or card (e.g credit card), may be temporarily suspended. If so, the following should apply (ref: [NIST 4.3](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/events/#loss-theft-damage-and-compromise)):

6.3.9 |  Verify that an administrator can suspend, invalidate, or destroy a user's authenticator when discovered to be compromised. | 2
-- | -- | --

To facilitate secure reporting, there is a need to establish an additional authenticator or backup (ref: [NIST 4.3](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/events/#loss-theft-damage-and-compromise)):

6.4.7 |  Verify that the user can securely report the authenticator as compromised or stolen using a backup or alternate single-factor authenticator in the case of compromise. | 2
-- | -- | --

It could, of course, be that the authenticator is only temporarily misplaced; if so, the service provider may support suspending the authenticator, and so reactivation should be allowed, but only after authentication (ref: [NIST 4.3](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/events/#loss-theft-damage-and-compromise)):

6.4.8 |  Verify that, in the case suspension of an authenticator is supported, it can be reactivated after the user has successfully authenticated using a non-suspended authenticator | 3
-- | -- | --

Finally, there are certain requirements regarding the binding itself (ref: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/events/#binding-across-endpoints):

6.4.9 |  Verify that in the case the new authenticator cannot be bound to the account automatically, the user must be activated either by using the new authenticator to request an activation code via an authenticated channel, or request an activation code through an authenticated channel and then use both the code and the new authenticator to complete activation.  | 3
-- | -- | --

-- | -- | --

There is also the issue of recovery of accounts that require MFA. (ref: [NIST 4.2.2](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/events/#recovery-requirements-by-ialaal))

6.4.10 |  Verify that, in the case multi-factor authentication is required, account recovery shall require the user to successfully provide two recovery codes from different sources, or provide one recovery code in addition to authenticating with a bound single-factor authenticator. | 3
-- | -- | --

Still, this is arguably covered by this:

6.4.4 | Verify that if a multi-factor authentication factor is lost, evidence of identity proofing is performed at the same level as during enrollment. | 2
-- | -- | --

I guess what I feel is missing in that sentence is perhaps more on the "enrollment" or binding phase. E.g: How does "binding" requirements uphold recovery requirements? If the binding requirements are not upheld, it's impossible to uphold recovery requirements, which means you quickly get into a situation where recovery becomes a way of bypassing MFA authentication. So, if MFA is required, there needs to be a strong policy requiring users to create backup measures.

6.4.10 |  Verify that the user is encouraged to maintain at least two separate means of authentication during the initial enrollment phase so that, in the case one is lost, authentication during recovery can be performed using multi-factor authentication. | 3
-- | -- | --

Under V6.4 we will need something like this:

In the event of loss, theft, damage, or compromise, a mechanism to revoke or suspend the authenticator immediately upon user notification is required. In the case suspension and reactivation is supported, the channel for notification and the process for reactivation must be implemented in such a way that account recovery does not reduce the required authentication strength and that recovery pathways uphold the same MFA guarantees as normal authentication without creating a mechanism for denial-of-service attacks.

See: [NIST 800-63-3: B.5.2](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3-Implementation-Resources/63B/Lifecycle/#s-b-5-2) and [NIST 800-63-3: 5.2.1](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#521-physical-authenticators)

Yes, I mentioned this requirement earlier with regard to activation that doesn't happen immediately upon onboarding.

### Problem

ASVS 6.4.4 requires identity proofing at the same level as enrollment when a multi-factor authentication (MFA) factor is lost. However, it does not cover cases where:

- An authenticator is a physical device that must be activated later, after the user has received it, e.g., key cards, identity cards, bank cards, etc.

This gap can lead to implementations where stolen authenticators can be used to gain unauthorized access to an application before the user receives them.

### Proposed Improvement

Clarify or extend existing requirements to mandate that:

- In the case that the authenticator can not be activated immediately, a process is in place to ensure the secure activation of the authenticator when the user receives it.

E.g:

6.4.9 | Verify that, in the case the new authenticator cannot be bound to the account automatically, the authenticator must be activated either by using the new authenticator to request activation and submitting proof of possession (activation code or crypographic proof ) via an authenticated channel, or request activation through an authenticated channel, providing the proof of possession and the new authenticator to complete activation. | 3
